title: Turn the AI policy into an enforced review rule with attestation
problem: Written AI policies have not on their own stopped unchecked AI output reaching courts; Butler Snow and Sullivan & Cromwell both had safeguards that failed.
approach: The policy names reviewers, requires independent verification of citations and outputs, limits tools, requires training first, and asks people to attest periodically.
Butler Snow lawyers were sanctioned in July 2025 despite a June 2023 policy; Sullivan & Cromwell said its protocols were not followed.
Morae survey: 71% have formal AI policies but 30% are confident they are applied (vendor-published).
The signing lawyer reviews all AI output and independently verifies citations before submission to a court.
who: Butler Snow, Sullivan & Cromwell, White & Case

title: Automated check of citations, quotations and cited propositions before signing
problem: Fabricated cases, altered quotations and real cases that do not support the stated point are hard to spot by eye.
approach: A checker extracts citations, compares them with a case-law corpus and flags what it cannot match; some test the cited proposition too.
A lawyer reviews each flagged citation in context; the signing lawyer, not the tool, decides whether to file.
Vendor back-test on 2,073 citations from 68 filings: 61.8% verified, 38.2% flagged (vendor-published; not an error rate for ordinary work).

title: Verification record on file: what was checked, by whom, and AI use
problem: Partners are sanctioned for citation errors they did not make, and firms need to know which parts of a deliverable involved AI and who reviewed them.
approach: Clearbrief's Cite Check Report, launched December 2025, lists each citation, flags problems, records how each was resolved and by whom.
Guidance suggests marking AI-generated material in files and documenting inputs, outputs and errors; no usage or effectiveness figure is published (vendor-published).
Reviewer records why a flag was ignored; the partner reviews the report before signing.

title: Idea: audit every reference and figure in AI-assisted consulting and advisory reports
problem: Between October 2025 and July 2026 reports from each Big Four firm were publicly questioned for fabricated or unverifiable citations, found by outsiders.
approach: Idea. A person who did not write the passage traces every footnote, quotation and calculation to its source; no firm does this.
The ICMCI code requires consultants to verify AI output independently; a second reader is suggested for high-stakes deliverables.
Deloitte agreed to repay the final instalment of an AUD 440,000 contract (independent); GPTZero claims 99 of 100 flawed citations caught (vendor-published).

title: Benchmark AI tools against expert answers to set review depth by task
problem: Vendors call their legal AI accurate or hallucination-free, and AI helps on some tasks but hurts on similar ones, so one review rule fits poorly.
approach: Linklaters built a 50-question English-law benchmark marked by senior lawyers; Vals ran studies with law-firm datasets and a lawyer baseline.
Linklaters' re-test scored OpenAI o1 at 6.4 out of 10 against Bard's 4.4 in 2023 (self-reported).
Vals: lawyers beat the best tool on redlining, 79.7% against 65.0%; the tool led on document Q&A (independent).
The firm sets permitted uses and review depth from results. A formal task map is an idea; no firm describes one.

title: Validate AI document review with test sets and sampling, not full re-reading
problem: AI document review can be wrong in issue-specific ways, formal statistical validation can be too slow, and re-reading every output removes the time saved.
approach: A Covington & Burling special counsel published a case study using Relativity aiR on 7,100 documents; a senior attorney tagged examples.
Issues 4 and 9 reached perfect performance by round four; issue 8 persistently produced higher false positives (self-reported).
Weak issues were supplemented with metadata and keyword searches; the team decides when prompt iteration shows diminishing returns.

title: Standing evaluation suites, gold-standard answers and change control run by legal engineers
problem: A firm deploying AI workflows needs to know whether each prompt, retrieval or model change improves or worsens the work, and who owns fixing errors.
approach: Latham & Watkins' job description has legal engineers build evaluation suites from real precedents, measure every change and keep audit trails.
Legora and Harvey advertise similar roles building gold-standard datasets and owning the quality bar for human evaluations.
Partners define the quality criteria; legal engineers validate against real matters. Job descriptions only, no results published (self-reported).

title: Review gates: a named reviewer signs off each AI step first
problem: Without forced checkpoints each reviewer may assume someone else validated an AI output, which Schellman's CEO calls a control design problem.
approach: Armanino gives each AI step its own controls, mirroring its technical-memo flow; the senior ticks a box confirming review before continuing.
Harvey's Legal Work Orchestration, announced 2026-10-15, holds the next step until the designated partner approves an agent-built consent matrix.
Harvey forecasts agents taking on an additional 20% of workflow steps in six months (vendor-published forecast); Armanino published no measures.

title: Idea: oversight tiered by agent autonomy, with escalation triggers and approval gates
problem: Idea at an early stage: agents can plan and finish tasks without prompting, raising the risk of unreviewed reliance and exposure of confidential information across matters.
approach: An Anthropic speaker at CLOC 2026 framed three designs: human in the loop, lawyer in the loop, and agent in the loop.
California's 2026 guidance says oversight must rise with autonomy, with no filing, advice or outside transmission without meaningful review.
Lawyer approves before any filing or outside transmission; autonomy is reassessed periodically. No error rates are published (vendor-published).

title: AI layer on the existing quality system with risk-tiered review
problem: Review can become accountability theater, with reviewers rubber-stamping, and the UK audit regulator found the six largest audit firms did not monitor tools' effect on quality.
approach: Forvis Mazars keeps its quality controls and adds AI requirements: planning discussion, reviewer checklists and independent review of every deliverable.
An engagement quality reviewer checks whether firm AI policy was followed on higher-risk audits.
Forvis Mazars describes zero tolerance for skipping review; no error figure (self-reported). The FRC found all six firms lacked formal monitoring (independent).

title: Track acceptance and overrides of AI output as a live quality signal
problem: Few firms track how often reviewers accept or reject AI output, so they cannot tell whether review catches errors or rubber-stamps.
approach: Microsoft's legal department uses its Legal Agent for contract review, with suggested edits as tracked changes that reviewers accept or reject.
Users kept roughly seven in ten suggestions, across about 100,000 edits and over 1,800 users (vendor-published).
Thomson Reuters Institute recommends tracking override patterns; the department reviews override patterns by area.

title: Idea: cut the verification tax with quick-check techniques for AI output
problem: Idea, not a deployment: many professionals fear the cost of checking AI outputs outweighs the benefit, and no measurement compares review time with drafting time saved.
approach: Idea. Teach teams quick, repeatable ways to verify AI output so review time falls without lowering the bar.
CLOC's May 2026 item promises quick verification techniques (teaser only). Morae survey: 67% fear checking costs outweigh benefits (vendor-published).
Written principles name who is accountable for outputs and where the lawyer intervenes.

title: Machine cross-check of AI output before human review
problem: Checking every reference by hand is slow and skimming reviewers miss near-match citations; this is an emerging approach with no published figures.
approach: Hacker News commenters proposed a sub-agent that validates references, with people reviewing only low-confidence items.
Litera announced in August 2026 that its Lito agent would build on its deterministic redline comparison engine, surfacing risky changes.
People verify flagged references and the lawyer reviews flagged changes; no accuracy figure is published for any design (vendor-published).

title: After an AI error is found, disclose, correct and re-review wider filings
problem: Once one fabricated citation is found, client, court and firm need to know whether others exist, and the response shapes the consequence.
approach: Sullivan & Cromwell's April 2026 letter took responsibility, filed a corrected motion with corrections schedule and re-reviewed all filings in the matter.
Butler Snow's outside counsel reviewed 2,400+ citations in 330 filings and found no further hallucinated citations (self-reported).
Deloitte Australia published a revised report disclosing Azure OpenAI use and repaid the final instalment. An outside reviewer conducts the look-back.
who: Sullivan & Cromwell, Butler Snow, Deloitte Australia

title: Check incoming work, including opponents' authorities and contractors' drafts
problem: In reported matters, fabricated authorities were found by opposing counsel or the judge, and errors also arrive through contractors' or other lawyers' work.
approach: Litigation teams check authorities cited against them; Boies Schiller Flexner flagged errors in Sullivan & Cromwell's filing. Contractor work is unverified.
BriefCatch and Thomson Reuters market tools for checking opponents' briefs.
In Noland, 21 of 23 quotations were fabricated and a $10,000 sanction followed (independent). Supervising lawyers verify everything returned before signing.
who: Boies Schiller Flexner, BriefCatch, Thomson Reuters

title: Tell clients when AI materially contributed and how the work was checked
problem: Clients increasingly ask whether AI was used on their work but are not consistently told, and disclosure rules differ.
approach: Forvis Mazars requires disclosure when AI materially contributed to external content; the ICMCI code and ABA Opinion 512 set related disclosure rules.
Morae survey: 73% say clients deserve full visibility into AI use, 21% deliver it (vendor-published).
ILTA: firms requiring client approval ranged from 8% to 38% by size (independent). A partner confirms disclosure language before delivery.

title: In-house teams set bounded AI workflows and ask outside firms for evidence
problem: In-house teams receive AI-assisted work from outside counsel and vendors but cannot see how it was checked.
approach: A Casepoint report says mature teams use bounded, reviewable workflows; Starbucks moved to controlled internal use while restricting vendor and outside-counsel use.
GSK and Ropes & Gray speakers say clients now ask firms what AI they use and whether it saves cost.
Thomson Reuters survey: 78% of corporate clients rate AI quality gains important, 6% say providers deliver them (vendor-published).

title: Idea-stage: documented AI governance ready for professional indemnity insurers
problem: Professional indemnity policies mostly ignore AI, but insurers are starting to ask how AI-enabled work is supervised; this is an emerging expectation.
approach: Firms keep records of AI use, protocols, verification standards and audit trails to answer insurer questions at proposal and renewal.
CPA-firm insurers say they ask whether firms use and police AI; a broker expects documented protocols within 12 to 18 months (forecast).
Risk or general counsel signs off proposal-form answers on AI use.
